newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland studies psychological damage from floods.
newsitem.headline: Poland studies psychological damage from floods.

text.p: Poland's health ministry sent teams of psychologists to flood-hit areas on Monday to decide how to tackle problems including depression, alcoholism and suicidal feelings now threatening some of the victims.
"We can expect some very disturbing phenomena such as a growth in alcoholism or drug abuse in these territories," said Professor Janusz Czapinski, coordinating psychological aid for flood victims.

He said in a radio interview that there were already signs of increased suicidal tendencies among people in the large areas devastated by the region's worst natural disaster in centuries, although no official statistics were yet available.
The month-long floods killed at least 54 people in Poland, affected some 2,600 towns and villages, forced 162,500 people to be evacuated and caused billions of dollars worth of damage.
Thousands of homes and farms have been devastated in the west and south, and huge tracts still remain flooded.
The ministry said last week that groups made up of psychologists, social workers and family doctors would offer help to all who needed it.

"The intervention groups...will ensure help to flood victims, especially those who suffered major material losses, lost the fruits of a lifetime's effort and above all those who suffered deep psychological traumas," it said in a statement.

Czapinski said the seven fact-finding teams visiting worst-hit areas of the south and west would meet in Warsaw on August 20 to collate information on needs and plan longer-term help, as well as proposals for action in future disasters.
For many survivors, the real psychological damage would start appearing now the immediate challenge of saving themselves and as much as possible of their property was over.
Physically and mentally exhausted people would be asking themselves whether the rest of their lifetimes would suffice to make up for everything they had lost, he said.

There was also likely to be a sense of injustice over the distribution of official aid -- for instance over who would benefit from at least 1,000 free houses the government is building for the neediest families made homeless in the floods.
"There could be a sense of wrong, of injustice, over the distribution of money or homes...this will create a climate of displeasure," Czapinski said.
He said survivors would need to talk of their experiences, and friends or relatives could help by listening.

The impact has been especially great on children, some of whom saw the security of their homes suddenly swept away while their parents were powerless against the destruction, and who suffer nightmares even now in refuges far from the flooding.
"I have heard of cases where children who are far away... wake in the night because of dreams that fill them with fear, and they talk endlessly about this misfortune," he said.
Czapinski said a handbook would be produced to help teachers in dealing with children seared by the experience.
